title: Rulers Die, but God Remains
overview: This psalm praises the LORD as the one lasting source of help, unlike human rulers who die, and lists the vulnerable people God takes care of.

parts.label: A lifelong song (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The singer urges their own inner self to praise God and promises to keep doing it for as long as they live. This psalm begins a group of five (Psalms 146 to 150) that open and close with the Hebrew call "Hallelujah," meaning "praise the LORD."

parts.label: Rulers are only human (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: Even powerful leaders are mortal: when their breath leaves, they return to the soil, and their plans end that same day. The point is not that leaders are bad, but that no person can carry anyone's ultimate hope, because no person lasts.

parts.label: The one worth trusting (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: "The God of Jacob" means the God of Israel's ancestor Jacob, and so the God of Israel's whole family story. He made sky, land and sea, and unlike rulers who die or break their word, he stays faithful forever.

parts.label: Who God looks after (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: The list names people who had no one to defend them in the ancient world: the oppressed, the hungry, prisoners, the blind, the crushed, foreigners, orphans and widows. Many readers see here what a good king was meant to do, and Christians later read it in light of Jesus, who described his own work in similar words (Matthew 11:5).

parts.label: A King who never dies (v. 10)
parts.note: Zion is the hill in Jerusalem where the temple stood, so it stands for God's people. The psalm ends by setting God's endless rule against the short lives of the rulers in verses 3 and 4.

think: What or who do you lean on that will not last forever, and how does knowing that shape the way you trust it?
